case_name: Donthula Ravindranath @ Ravinder Rao v State of Andhra Pradesh
respondent:
State of Andhra Pradesh
Supreme Court of India

6 January 2014
Cr.A. No. 594 of 2009
(Non-Reportable)
The Judgment was delivered by : J. Chelameswar, J.
1. This is an appeal against the judgment of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh in Criminal Appeal No.203 of 2005 dated 5th June 2007. By the said judgment, the High Court confirmed the judgment dated 8th February 2005 in Sessions Case No.23 of 2004 on the file of the V-Addl. Sessions Judge (Fast Track Court) at Nizamabad.
2. The sole appellant herein alongwith his parents was tried for the offences under section 304B and 498A IPC. Apart from that the appellant herein was tried for an offence u/s. 302 IPC simplicitor while all the three persons were charged and tried for the offence u/s. 302 read with s. 109 IPC. facts: This is an appeal against the judgment of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh in Criminal Appeal No.203 of 2005 dated 5th June 2007.
The sole appellant herein alongwith his parents was tried for the offences under section 304B and 498A IPC.
The wife of the appellant by name Jyotsna died on 21st May 2003.
The prosecution case rested on the circumstantial evidence.
To establish the above circumstances the prosecution examined as many as 16 witnesses.
According to the evidence of PW1, some unknown person had informed by telephone on the fateful day in the morning hours that the deceased was ill.
The learned counsel for the appellant argued that there is no iota of evidence to establish that the appellant caused the death of Jyotsna.
The learned counsel made elaborate submissions impeaching the credibility of the evidence of PW14 the doctor who conducted the post mortem examination.

On the other hand, the learned counsel for the State argued that the concurrent finding of fact resulting in the conviction of the appellant u/s. 302 IPC may not be interfered with in the absence of any illegality in the judgment under appeal.
The third circumstance relied upon by the prosecution is that the deceased was harassed by the appellant for additional dowry.

The fourth circumstance that the death of Jyotsna in the opinion [of the doctor] was caused by strangulation (we do not propose to examine the correctness of the opinion) even if believed need not, in our opinion, lead to the conclusion that it is only the accused who must be held responsible for such strangulation.

All the ingredients of section 304B are satisfied in the instant case, that the death of Jyotsna occurred within seven years of her marriage the death occurred otherwise than under normal circumstances and that Jyotsna was subjected to harassment which amounted to cruelty within the meaning of section 498A IPC of which charge the appellant is also found guilty by both the courts below.
In the light of the abovementioned circumstances, the appellant in our opinion must be found guilty for an offence under section 304B IPC.
issues: What is the evidence that establishes the guilt of the accused?
Can the conviction of the accused be interfered with in the absence of any illegality in the judgment under appeal?
What is the significance of the extra-judicial confession made by the appellant before PW9?
petitioner_arguments: There is no iota of evidence to establish that the appellant caused the death of Jyotsna.

The prosecution must establish the guilt of accused beyond all reasonable doubt and in a case of circumstantial evidence the chain of circumstances is so complete that they collectively point only to the guilt of the accused without leaving any scope for doubt.

Having regard to the nature of the external injuries on the body of the deceased, the death of Jyotsna is a result of hanging but not strangulation thereby creating doubt about the credibility of the prosecution case.
respondent_arguments: The concurrent finding of fact resulting in the conviction of the appellant u/s. 302 IPC may not be interfered with in the absence of any illegality in the judgment under appeal.

The death of Jyotsna occurred within seven years of her marriage the death occurred otherwise than under normal circumstances and that Jyotsna was subjected to harassment which amounted to cruelty within the meaning of section 498A IPC of which charge the appellant is also found guilty by both the courts below.
court_reasoning: One of the five circumstances relied upon by the prosecution to establish the guilt of the accused i.e. the alleged extra-judicial confession made by the appellant before PW9 is disbelieved by the High Court.
Therefore, only four circumstances remain, they are: (i) the appellant and the deceased were husband and wife; and (ii) they were living in the same house.
These facts are not even disputed by the appellant.
The third circumstance relied upon by the prosecution is that the deceased was harassed by the appellant for additional dowry.

The fourth circumstance that the death of Jyotsna in the opinion [of the doctor] was caused by strangulation (we do not propose to examine the correctness of the opinion) even if believed need not, in our opinion, lead to the conclusion that it is only the accused who must be held responsible for such strangulation.

All the ingredients of section 304B are satisfied in the instant case, that the death of Jyotsna occurred within seven years of her marriage the death occurred otherwise than under normal circumstances and that Jyotsna was subjected to harassment which amounted to cruelty within the meaning of section 498A IPC of which charge the appellant is also found guilty by both the courts below.
In the light of the abovementioned circumstances, the appellant in our opinion must be found guilty for an offence under section 304B IPC.
holding: The judgment under appeal is modified accordingly. Order accordingly.
